module_title: States of Matter & Solid State Basics (Detailed Foundational)
introduction: This foundational level establishes the macroscopic properties of gases and the structural classification of solids. It covers the empirical gas laws that led to the Ideal Gas Equation, Dalton's Law of partial pressures, and the fundamental geometries of crystalline unit cells (SC, BCC, FCC). Mastery here guarantees marks in direct formula-based questions.

core_concepts.title: Empirical Gas Laws
core_concepts.description:
1. Boyle's Law ($T$ constant): Pressure is inversely proportional to volume. $P \propto 1/V \Rightarrow P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$.
2. Charles's Law ($P$ constant): Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature. $V \propto T \Rightarrow V_1/T_1 = V_2/T_2$.
3. Gay-Lussac's Law ($V$ constant): Pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature. $P \propto T \Rightarrow P_1/T_1 = P_2/T_2$.
4. Avogadro's Law ($T, P$ constant): Volume is directly proportional to the number of moles. $V \propto n$.

core_concepts.title: The Ideal Gas Equation
core_concepts.description: Combining all empirical laws yields the universal state equation for an ideal gas: $PV = nRT$. Here, $R$ is the Universal Gas Constant. Its value depends on the units of $P$ and $V$: $R = 0.0821 \text{ L atm K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$ or $R = 8.314 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$. The density form of this equation is $PM = dRT$, where $M$ is molar mass and $d$ is density.

core_concepts.title: Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures
core_concepts.description: In a mixture of non-reacting gases, the total pressure exerted is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of individual gases. $P_{\text{total}} = p_1 + p_2 + p_3 + ...$. The partial pressure of any component can be found using its mole fraction ($x_i$): $p_i = x_i \times P_{\text{total}}$.

core_concepts.title: Classification of Solids
core_concepts.description:
1. Crystalline Solids: Have a highly regular, repeating 3D arrangement of particles (long-range order). They possess sharp melting points and are Anisotropic (physical properties vary with direction). Examples: NaCl, Diamond, Quartz.
2. Amorphous Solids: Lack a regular arrangement (short-range order only). They soften over a range of temperatures and are Isotropic (properties are identical in all directions). Examples: Glass, Rubber, Plastics. Glass is often termed a 'supercooled liquid' or pseudo-solid.

core_concepts.title: Unit Cells and Effective Number of Atoms ($Z$)
core_concepts.description:
A unit cell is the smallest repeating building block of a crystal lattice. 
1. Simple Cubic (SC): Atoms at 8 corners. Contribution per corner is $1/8$. Total atoms $Z = 8 \times (1/8) = 1$.
2. Body-Centered Cubic (BCC): Atoms at 8 corners + 1 at body center. $Z = (8 \times 1/8) + 1 = 2$.
3. Face-Centered Cubic (FCC / CCP): Atoms at 8 corners + 6 face centers (contribution $1/2$). $Z = (8 \times 1/8) + (6 \times 1/2) = 4$.

important_entities.name: Standard Temperature and Pressure (STP vs SATP)
important_entities.key_fact: STP uses $1 \text{ atm}$, SATP uses $1 \text{ bar}$.
important_entities.significance: Under the older STP conditions ($0^\circ\text{C}$ and $1 \text{ atm}$), the molar volume of an ideal gas is exactly $22.4 \text{ L}$. Under modern SATP conditions ($25^\circ\text{C}$ and $1 \text{ bar}$), it is $\approx 24.8 \text{ L}$. If a NEET/JEE question specifies $273 \text{ K}$ and $1 \text{ bar}$, the volume is $22.7 \text{ L}$. Always check the pressure unit!

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: Temperature Unit Trap in Gas Laws
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: In all gas law calculations (Charles's, Gay-Lussac's, Ideal Gas), the temperature $T$ MUST be in Kelvin (Absolute Temperature). If you plug Celsius values directly into $V_1/T_1 = V_2/T_2$, you will mathematically get an entirely incorrect answer, and examiners always include this wrong answer as an option.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation:
To remember which variable is constant in which law: 
Boyle's Law: Think of 'Boil' $\rightarrow$ boiling relates to Temperature. So, Temperature ($T$) is constant.
Charles's Law: Think of 'Prince Charles is under Pressure'. So, Pressure ($P$) is constant.

exam_strategy_tips: When collecting a gas over water in a lab (e.g., $O_2$ collection), the measured pressure is the total pressure of the wet gas. To find the pressure of the dry gas for stoichiometry, you must subtract the aqueous tension (vapor pressure of water at that temperature): $P_{\text{dry gas}} = P_{\text{total}} - P_{\text{aqueous tension}}$.
